title: Conquering Agent Chaos — Rick Blalock, Agentuity

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling

summary: Rick Blalock from Agentuity addresses the pervasive challenges of deploying and running AI agents, drawing on his own experience and that of University of Florida students and professors who universally cited deployment as their top problem. Core deployment headaches include serverless platform timeouts (AWS Lambda), with agents needing 15-40 minutes of runtime; inability to use VMs or EC2 in some environments; gateway issues wiring agents to communicate; and the fundamental mismatch between the web's stateless architecture and agents' inherently stateful nature. Blalock had the same experience building a qualitative research agent set that required re-architecting away from serverless. He identifies what agents need to succeed: ability to run as long as needed, pause and resume, decouple inputs and outputs from code, support multiple input/output types, introspection, self-observability and self-reflection (distinct from human-oriented tracing), memory, evolution, and code execution. The Agentuity platform demo shows a CLI-based workflow: 'agentuity create' scaffolds a project supporting three runtimes (Bun, Python with UV, Node.js) and multiple framework templates (Mastra, Vercel AI SDK, Grok, Crew AI, LangChain, Pydantic). The platform is framework-agnostic, allowing agents built with different frameworks to communicate via internal networking. Dev mode includes a simulator supporting text, JSON, HTML, and PDF inputs, plus log inspection and session-level observability showing costs, prompts, and responses through an AI gateway that eliminates manual model API key setup. Code conventions are minimal: a YAML config file, an agents folder, and an entry point. Deployment wraps agents in specialized containers and surfaces cost breakdowns. Agents can receive inputs via email, SMS, APIs, and cron jobs. A live webhook demo creates a session but encounters a memory footprint error configurable via YAML. Blalock notes 50-60 internal agents built on the platform, with upcoming infrastructure agents that watch logs and surface issues—joking they should call it 'agent duty, not PagerDuty.' He also confirms interest in tool calling within reasoning for a CRM agent use case, and envisions offering agent-success capabilities as a services layer.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Deployment Headaches
sections.summary: Blalock introduces himself and Agentuity, then describes the universal problem of agent deployment. He cites University of Florida students and professors who all identified deployment as their top challenge, specifically serverless timeouts on AWS Lambda (agents needing 15-40 minutes), inability to use VMs/EC2, gateway issues wiring agents together, and the mismatch between stateless web architecture and stateful agents.

sections.title: What Agents Need to Be Successful
sections.summary: Blalock outlines the core requirements for successful agents: running as long as needed, pause/stop/resume capability, decoupled inputs and outputs (multiple types), introspection, self-observability, self-reflection, memory, evolution, and code execution. He distinguishes human-oriented observability (traces, spans) from agent-oriented self-observability, noting agents need to understand their own observability data.

sections.title: Demo: Creating a Project
sections.summary: Live demo begins with 'agentuity create' CLI. Three runtimes supported: Bun, Python with UV (biased over pip), Node.js. Multiple framework templates available including Mastra, Vercel AI SDK, Grok, Crew AI, LangChain, Pydantic. Platform is framework-agnostic with inter-agent communication. Projects map to repos with optional GitHub auto-deploy. Agents are first-class infrastructure citizens with routing, per-agent API keys, and project-level protection.

sections.title: Dev Mode and Simulator
sections.summary: Dev mode runs locally with 'agentuity dev', assigning ports for multiple projects and providing public tunneling. A simulator supports text, JSON, HTML, and PDF inputs. Log inspection and session-level observability show AI gateway calls with cost, prompt, and response details. The AI gateway eliminates manual model API key setup. Dev mode mirrors production.

sections.title: Code Conventions
sections.summary: Minimal conventions: a YAML config file, an agents folder, and an entry point (default export in JS, run function in Python). The context object provides ctx.get_agent to retrieve other agents by ID or name with ephemeral tokens for inter-agent communication. Framework-specific code (Mastra, Crew AI, Pydantic) can be dropped into the entry point.

sections.title: Deployment and Agent Inputs
sections.summary: Live deployment wraps the agent in a specialized Bun container. The platform surfaces cost breakdowns by project, agent, and run. Agents can receive inputs beyond HTTP: email addresses, SMS, APIs, and cron jobs can be added via the platform UI, demonstrating decoupled input/output capability.

sections.title: Webhook Demo, Future Plans, and Q&A
sections.summary: Blalock demonstrates hitting a public webhook on the deployed agent, creating a session with a session ID. The agent errors due to insufficient memory footprint, which is configurable in the YAML file. He mentions upcoming integrations (GitHub, Slack, Discord) and notes 50-60 internal agents built on the platform. Future plans include infrastructure agents that watch logs and surface issues—joking about calling it 'agent duty, not PagerDuty'—and a services layer offering agent-success capabilities out of the box. In Q&A, he confirms interest in tool calling within reasoning for a CRM agent use case.
